For \(n=365\), the leading scale \(365\log365\) is approximately
\(2153.46\), while the exact finite expectation \(365H_{365}\) is

text:
For the source's concrete case \(n=365\)
\cite[Example~2.2.7, p.~60]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}, a coupon is a
birthday: when the birthdays of the people one meets are i.i.d. and
uniform over \(365\) days, \(T_{365}\) is the number of people one
has to meet before each of the \(365\) birthdays has occurred. The
source reads the limit theorem as saying that a complete set takes
about \(365\log365=2153.46\) tries, and it notes that the count of
trials is \(5.89\) times as large as the number of birthdays. That
ratio is \(\log365=5.8998\ldots\); the source's \(5.89\) truncates it,
and rounding to two decimal places gives \(5.90\). This reading uses
the leading scale \(n\log n\) of the weak law, not the expectation:
the exact finite expectation \(365H_{365}\) is approximately
\(2364.65\), which is \(H_{365}\approx6.48\) times the number of
birthdays. These are distinct quantities in the specified
uniform-coupon model. The weak law states only that
\(T_n/(n\log n)\) is near \(1\) with probability tending to \(1\) as
\(n\to\infty\); it gives no error bound at \(n=365\).

The replacement supplies the birthday reading, the 'about 2153.46 tries' claim and the 5.89 ratio with its exact value log 365 = 5.8998..., and keeps the exact-expectation qualification (365 H_365 ~ 2364.65).
